fields.lead: The field is mainly working on why democracies erode from within and how modern autocracies use elections, parties and repression to survive.

papers.title: Some Social Requisites of Democracy: Economic Development and Political Legitimacy
papers.why: Tied democracy to wealth, education and legitimacy, setting up the modernization hypothesis. Every new study of whether rich democracies can backslide is still testing Lipset's claim.

papers.title: The Perils of Presidentialism
papers.why: Argued that fixed terms and dual legitimacy make presidential systems more breakdown-prone than parliamentary ones. The claim is still debated whenever presidents push past constraints, from Latin America to the US.

papers.title: Modernization: Theories and Facts
papers.why: Separated two ideas: wealth may not cause democratization, but it strongly protects democracies that already exist. That distinction frames today's surprise at backsliding in middle- and high-income democracies.

papers.title: Endogenous Democratization
papers.why: Pushed back on Przeworski and Limongi with longer data, arguing development does cause democratization. Together the two papers are the live core of the modernization debate.

papers.title: Increasing Returns, Path Dependence, and the Study of Politics
papers.why: Gave a precise account of why early institutional choices lock in and become costly to reverse. It underpins much current historical-institutional work on long-run legacies and critical junctures.

papers.title: Ethnicity, Insurgency, and Civil War
papers.why: Found that weak states, poverty and rough terrain, not ethnic diversity or grievance, predict civil war onset. It remains the benchmark that newer grievance and exclusion arguments must beat.

papers.title: The Rise of Competitive Authoritarianism
papers.why: Named the hybrid regime that holds real elections on a tilted playing field. The concept is now the standard lens for Hungary, Turkey, Venezuela and similar cases.

papers.title: Credible Power-Sharing and the Longevity of Authoritarian Rule
papers.why: Showed how ruling parties let dictators credibly share spoils with elites and so survive longer. It is central to the current study of why some autocracies are so durable.

papers.title: On Democratic Backsliding
papers.why: Showed that democracies now rarely die by coup and instead erode through elected executives' gradual aggrandizement. That reframing defines the backsliding research agenda.

papers.title: Polarization versus Democracy
papers.why: Argued that polarized voters will tolerate undemocratic behavior by their own side, so elections stop checking would-be autocrats. It drives current experimental work on voters as a democratic safeguard.

more.title: What Do We Know About Democratization After Twenty Years?
more.why: Introduced the split between military, single-party and personalist regimes and showed they break down differently. Her typology and data still structure most quantitative work on autocracy.

more.title: Clientelism and Voting: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Benin
more.why: Ran real campaign experiments to show clientelist promises beat programmatic ones. It opened the door to field experiments on clientelism and vote buying across the developing world.

more.title: The Political Salience of Cultural Difference: Why Chewas and Tumbukas Are Allies in Malawi and Adversaries in Zambia
more.why: Used a natural experiment to show ethnic divisions matter politically only when groups are big enough to be useful coalitions. It anchors the constructivist view of ethnic politics.

more.title: Authoritarian Institutions and the Survival of Autocrats
more.why: Argued that dictators create legislatures and parties to co-opt opponents, and that this helps them last. It launched the 'authoritarian institutions' literature that is still expanding.

more.title: Power Sharing and Leadership Dynamics in Authoritarian Regimes
more.why: Modeled the dictator-elite struggle and explained why most autocrats fall to insiders rather than mass revolt. The framework is widely used in work on coups and personalization.

more.title: Why Do Ethnic Groups Rebel? New Data and Analysis
more.why: Using new data on ethnic power relations, showed that groups excluded from state power are far more likely to rebel. It reopened the grievance debate against Fearon and Laitin.

more.title: How Censorship in China Allows Government Criticism but Silences Collective Expression
more.why: Found that Chinese censors tolerate criticism but delete anything that could spark collective action. It set the agenda for studying digital authoritarianism.

more.title: The Danger of Deconsolidation: The Democratic Disconnect
more.why: Claimed that support for democracy is falling among younger citizens in established democracies. The claim and its rebuttals remain a live argument about whether democratic values are eroding.
more.note: Subtitle wording 'The Democratic Disconnect' is from memory.

more.title: A Third Wave of Autocratization Is Here: What Is New About It?
more.why: Used V-Dem data to document a global wave of democratic decline led by gradual erosion under legal cover. It is the standard empirical reference for the scale of current backsliding.

more.title: Democracy in America? Partisanship, Polarization, and the Robustness of Support for Democracy in the United States
more.why: Showed experimentally that only a small share of Americans punish their own candidate for undemocratic acts. It is a key piece of evidence on why voters fail to check backsliding.

fields.lead: The field is mainly working on how shifting power, domestic politics and economic interdependence shape war, coercion and the durability of international order.

papers.title: Cooperation Under the Security Dilemma
papers.why: Showed that defensive moves can look offensive, so states can spiral into conflict nobody wants, and that the offense-defense balance changes the odds. It still frames debates on arms races, cyber and US-China competition.

papers.title: Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs
papers.why: Revived Kant's argument that liberal states do not fight each other while remaining aggressive toward others. The democratic peace it launched is still tested and contested.

papers.title: Diplomacy and Domestic Politics: The Logic of Two-Level Games
papers.why: Modeled leaders as bargaining at once with foreign counterparts and domestic ratifiers. The two-level frame is standard in work on trade deals, climate talks and sanctions.

papers.title: Anarchy Is What States Make of It: The Social Construction of Power Politics
papers.why: Argued that anarchy has no fixed logic; self-help depends on how states come to see each other. It founded mainstream constructivism, which still contests realist and rationalist work.

papers.title: The False Promise of International Institutions
papers.why: Argued that institutions merely reflect power and cannot cause peace. Its challenge returns whenever great-power rivalry strains the liberal order.

papers.title: Rationalist Explanations for War
papers.why: Asked why rational states fight when a bargain would be cheaper, and answered with private information, commitment problems and indivisibility. Nearly all formal and much empirical conflict research starts here.

papers.title: Taking Preferences Seriously: A Liberal Theory of International Politics
papers.why: Rebuilt liberalism around the domestic preferences that states bring to the table. It shaped the field's move toward domestic-politics explanations of foreign policy.

papers.title: The Rational Design of International Institutions
papers.why: Treated features like membership, scope and flexibility as rational responses to cooperation problems. It is the baseline for current work on treaty design and institutional change.

papers.title: Domestic Audience Costs in International Relations: An Experimental Approach
papers.why: Used survey experiments to show citizens punish leaders who back down from threats. It made experiments a core IR method and anchors the audience-cost debate.

papers.title: Why Civil Resistance Works: The Strategic Logic of Nonviolent Conflict
papers.why: Found nonviolent campaigns succeeded about twice as often as violent ones because they draw broader participation. Researchers are now actively testing why that success rate has fallen.

more.title: Theory of International Politics
more.why: Built structural realism: the distribution of power among states, not their character, drives their behavior. It is still the theory that rising-power and polarity arguments return to.

more.title: After Hegemony: Cooperation and Discord in the World Political Economy
more.why: Showed how institutions can sustain cooperation by cutting transaction costs even as a hegemon declines. It bears directly on whether today's order survives US relative decline.

more.title: Domestic Political Audiences and the Escalation of International Disputes
more.why: Introduced audience costs: leaders who back down face domestic punishment, which makes their threats credible. The idea is still tested, extended and challenged.

more.title: The Critical Barrier to Civil War Settlement
more.why: Argued that civil wars rarely end in settlements because rebels cannot safely disarm without outside guarantees. It shaped research and policy on peacekeeping and peace deals.

more.title: International Norm Dynamics and Political Change
more.why: Described the norm 'life cycle' from emergence to cascade to internalization. It remains the main framework for studying how human-rights and other norms spread and erode.

more.title: War as a Commitment Problem
more.why: Showed that large, rapid shifts in power make bargains impossible to commit to, which can cause war. It is central to analysis of rising powers and preventive war.

more.title: The Capitalist Peace
more.why: Argued that market development and shared interests, not democracy, explain peace among developed states. It is a main rival to democratic-peace explanations.

more.title: Autocratic Audience Costs: Regime Type and Signaling Resolve
more.why: Showed that many autocracies also face elite audiences who punish backing down. It broadened audience-cost theory beyond democracies and shaped work on autocratic foreign policy.

more.title: Known Unknowns: Power Shifts, Uncertainty, and War
more.why: Argued that wars over power shifts arise when one side cannot observe the other's military investments. It sharpens the commitment-problem account for cases like nuclear proliferation.

more.title: Weaponized Interdependence: How Global Economic Networks Shape State Coercion
more.why: Showed how states that control hubs in finance and information networks can use them to coerce others. It is now the core frame for sanctions, export controls and US-China tech competition.

fields.lead: The field is mainly working on how inequality, trade and financial shocks feed populism and polarization, and how institutions shape long-run development.

papers.title: A Rational Theory of the Size of Government
papers.why: Predicted that more inequality leads the median voter to demand more redistribution. The puzzle that rising inequality has not reliably raised redistribution keeps it at the center of debate.

papers.title: Constitutions and Commitment: The Evolution of Institutions Governing Public Choice in Seventeenth-Century England
papers.why: Argued that the Glorious Revolution made the crown's promises credible and so opened cheap credit and growth. Its theory of credible commitment is still built on and historically contested.

papers.title: Protection for Sale
papers.why: Modeled trade policy as the outcome of lobbies bidding for protection. It remains the workhorse model of interest groups and trade policy.

papers.title: Why Did the West Extend the Franchise? Democracy, Inequality, and Growth in Historical Perspective
papers.why: Argued that elites extended voting rights to commit credibly to redistribution under threat of revolution. It is central to current models of democratization and redistribution.

papers.title: The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation
papers.why: Used settler mortality to argue that institutions cause long-run prosperity. The paper, its instrument and its critics still define the institutions-versus-geography debate.

papers.title: An Asset Theory of Social Policy Preferences
papers.why: Argued that workers with specific skills want social insurance because their skills are hard to move. It is a basis for current work on how automation and skills shape welfare politics.

papers.title: What Determines Individual Trade-Policy Preferences?
papers.why: Showed that less-skilled US workers oppose trade, consistent with factor-based theory. It sets the material-interest baseline that newer identity-based accounts argue against.

papers.title: Going to Extremes: Politics after Financial Crises, 1870–2014
papers.why: Found that far-right vote shares rise sharply after financial crises across nearly 150 years of data. It is a key reference on the economic roots of populism.

papers.title: Democracy Does Cause Growth
papers.why: Found that democratization raises GDP per capita by about 20% over the long run. It answered a long-unsettled question and is now the reference point for democracy-growth claims.

papers.title: Importing Political Polarization? The Electoral Consequences of Rising Trade Exposure
papers.why: Linked local exposure to Chinese imports to ideological polarization and gains for more extreme candidates. It is central to the debate on the economic causes of polarization.

more.title: Dictatorship, Democracy, and Development
more.why: Contrasted 'roving' and 'stationary' bandits to explain why rulers who expect to stay provide order and growth. It still informs work on autocratic time horizons and development.

more.title: Why Do More Open Economies Have Bigger Governments?
more.why: Showed that more trade-exposed countries have larger governments, as insurance against external risk. It underlies the 'embedded liberalism' account of the globalization backlash.

more.title: Why Doesn't the United States Have a European-Style Welfare State?
more.why: Attributed the gap to political institutions and racial heterogeneity more than economics. It drives current research on race, diversity and support for redistribution.

more.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
more.why: Showed that campaign contributions are small relative to the stakes and look more like consumption than investment. It remains the starting point for debates about money and policy influence.

more.title: The Long-Term Effects of Africa's Slave Trades
more.why: Found that African regions hit hardest by the slave trades are poorer today. It helped found the historical-persistence literature now central to political economy.

more.title: The Origins of State Capacity: Property Rights, Taxation, and Politics
more.why: Modeled state capacity as an investment that governments choose to make. It launched the state-capacity research agenda.

more.title: The Persistent Effects of Peru's Mining Mita
more.why: Used a regression-discontinuity design at a colonial boundary to show forced labor still lowers living standards. It set the methodological standard for persistence studies.

more.title: The Trade Origins of Economic Nationalism: Import Competition and Voting Behavior in Western Europe
more.why: Showed that regions hit harder by Chinese imports shifted toward nationalist and radical-right parties. It extended the China-shock politics findings to Europe.

more.title: Brahmin Left Versus Merchant Right: Changing Political Cleavages in 21 Western Democracies, 1948–2020
more.why: Documented the shift of highly educated voters to the left while high-income voters stay right. It is a key data source for current debates on class, education and realignment.

more.title: The Political Economy of Populism
more.why: Surveys the evidence on economic and cultural causes of populism. It is the current map of the field's most active debate.

fields.lead: The field is mainly working on affective polarization, the limits of persuasion and misinformation, and how far governments respond to ordinary voters.

papers.title: The Nature of Belief Systems in Mass Publics
papers.venue: In D. Apter (ed.), Ideology and Discontent, Free Press
papers.why: Found most citizens hold weak, inconsistent policy views and do not think in ideological terms. Research on ideology, polarization and voter competence is still arguing with it.

papers.title: Effects of Public Opinion on Policy
papers.why: Found that policy tends to move with large shifts in public opinion. It set up the responsiveness question that Gilens and Page and others reopened.

papers.title: A Simple Theory of the Survey Response: Answering Questions versus Revealing Preferences
papers.why: Argued that survey answers are samples from the considerations at the top of the head, not fixed attitudes. It still shapes how researchers interpret opinion data and framing effects.

papers.title: The Effects of Canvassing, Telephone Calls, and Direct Mail on Voter Turnout: A Field Experiment
papers.why: Ran large field experiments showing door-to-door canvassing raises turnout while mail and calls do little. It launched the experimental turn in political behavior.

papers.title: Motivated Skepticism in the Evaluation of Political Beliefs
papers.why: Showed people accept congenial arguments and scrutinize opposing ones, so exposure can deepen disagreement. It drives current work on motivated reasoning and corrections.

papers.title: Affect, Not Ideology: A Social Identity Perspective on Polarization
papers.why: Showed that partisans increasingly dislike the other party even without ideological divergence. It launched the affective-polarization literature, now one of the field's largest.

papers.title: Testing Theories of American Politics: Elites, Interest Groups, and Average Citizens
papers.why: Found US policy tracks the preferences of affluent citizens and organized groups, not average voters. Its claims and methods are still actively debated.

papers.title: I Disrespectfully Agree: The Differential Effects of Partisan Sorting on Social and Issue Polarization
papers.why: Showed partisan-ideological sorting raises anger and bias even when policy views do not diverge. It is a core account of identity-based polarization.

papers.title: Democracy for Realists: Why Elections Do Not Produce Responsive Government
papers.why: Argued that voters act on group identity and punish incumbents for things beyond their control. It is the main recent challenge to standard theories of democratic accountability.

papers.title: The Minimal Persuasive Effects of Campaign Contact in General Elections: Evidence from 49 Field Experiments
papers.why: Found the average persuasive effect of campaign contact in general elections is close to zero. It reset expectations about what campaigns can achieve.

more.title: The American Voter
more.why: Argued that party identification is a stable, early-learned attachment that colors how voters see politics. The identity view of partisanship that dominates today descends from it.

more.title: Beyond the Running Tally: Partisan Bias in Political Perceptions
more.why: Showed partisans perceive basic economic facts differently. It is a foundation for research on partisan bias in factual beliefs.

more.title: Irrelevant Events Affect Voters' Evaluations of Government Performance
more.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
more.why: Found local college football wins boost incumbent vote shares. It is a key piece of evidence in the debate over blind retrospection.

more.title: When Corrections Fail: The Persistence of Political Misperceptions
more.why: Reported that corrections can sometimes strengthen misperceptions, the 'backfire effect'. It launched the misinformation-correction literature.

more.title: Follow the Leader? How Voters Respond to Politicians' Policies and Performance
more.why: Showed voters often adopt their party's positions rather than choosing parties based on policy. It is central to debates on whether voters hold leaders accountable on issues.

more.title: Partisan Bias in Factual Beliefs about Politics
more.why: Showed that paying people for correct answers shrinks partisan gaps in factual beliefs. It raised the question of how much partisan bias is expressive cheerleading.

more.title: Durably Reducing Transphobia: A Field Experiment on Door-to-Door Canvassing
more.why: Found that brief perspective-taking conversations produced lasting attitude change. It revived research on 'deep canvassing' and durable persuasion.

more.title: The Elusive Backfire Effect: Mass Attitudes' Steadfast Factual Adherence
more.why: Across many experiments, found that corrections rarely backfire and usually work. It largely overturned the backfire consensus.

more.title: The Origins and Consequences of Affective Polarization in the United States
more.why: Synthesizes evidence on why partisan animosity has grown and what it does. It is the standard map of the affective-polarization field.

more.title: Exposure to Untrustworthy Websites in the 2016 US Election
more.why: Using browsing data, found fake-news exposure was concentrated in a small, older, highly partisan group. It anchors current measurement-based work on misinformation.
